Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Orchestrator - BlogblogBlogBlogGemini 4 Hydrogen and Orchestrator - Blog

Today, we’re rolling out Gemini 4 Hydrogen inside Google Antigravity alongside a new model dropdown option called Orchestrator, which pairs Hydrogen with Gemini 4 Carbon in an optimized balance of quality, efficiency, and latency.

Selecting Orchestrator from the model selector in Google Antigravity.

Put Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen to work with Orchestrator

Earlier this week, we introduced Gemini 4 Carbon alongside /swarm for tackling massive, multi-worktree engineering tasks with parallel agent teams. In just a couple of days, tens of thousands of swarms have been launched on Antigravity, pushing frontier intelligence on the hardest problems.

For everyday feature work and debugging inside a single session, running a frontier reasoning model with multiple parallel agents on every step of every routine task slows down your loop and burns frontier quota. A common industry approach is to use a static “model router” that guesses task difficulty from your first prompt and routes the entire task to the cheapest model that is good enough to complete the task. Unfortunately, these start breaking down as agents become longer running, requiring different levels of complexity at different stages, often discovered as the task evolves.

Orchestrator takes a dynamic, bidirectional approach between Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen within the evolution of a single trajectory. For example, Carbon can start in a read-only phase to explore dependencies, resolve ambiguities, and build a concrete plan with explicit re-planning triggers. Hydrogen could then take over to write edits, update packages, and run tests. If Hydrogen hits friction, it would hand back to Carbon to inspect the state, repair the plan, and resume execution. This allows Orchestrator to reach near-Carbon task success while being faster and more quota-efficient. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster.

  • Explicit multi-model pipelines with the Antigravity SDK: When you want programmatic control over which model handles each role, you can wire Hydrogen and Carbon together directly with the Antigravity SDK. In the demo below, an open-source issue triage system built with the Antigravity SDK pairs multiple agents together. The Hydrogen agents handle triaging and coding to keep up with incoming issue volume, searching the codebase, asking clarifying questions, and fast UI iteration from PR comments while the Carbon agent is assigned to larger refactors, new features, and security checks.

Pairing Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon with the Antigravity SDK for automated open-source issue triage and code generation.

  • Fast, dependable execution with Gemini 4 Hydrogen: Hydrogen also works as a standalone model for everyday coding and agentic work, scoring 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (surpassing Argon’s 50, and reaching 54 at its highest setting) and 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 (more than tripiling 3.8 Flash’s 18.2%). When selecting Hydrogen directly, you can dial reasoning depth across four thinking levels, low, medium, high (default), and a new xhigh tier.

Using Gemini 4 Hydrogen in Google Antigravity to upgrade dependencies, refactor shared utilities, and generate accessible image alt text.

Getting started

Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings cutting-edge intelligence for everyday coding and agentic workflows. When you want frontier planning paired with speed without managing model switches, Orchestrator puts both Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen behind one prompt. Starting today, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is rolling out across paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Orchestrator is rolling out for Google AI Ultra subscribers, with additional models and plans supported in the future. Enterprises can access both in Gemini for business.

item.title: Rust 1.100 (118 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/11/12/Rust-1.100.0/, See on Hacker News

The Rust team is happy to announce a new version of Rust, 1.100.0. Rust is a programming language empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software.

If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup, you can get 1.100.0 with:

$ rustup update stable

If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website, and check out the detailed release notes for 1.100.0.

If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider updating locally to use the beta channel (rustup default beta) or the nightly channel (rustup default nightly). Please report any bugs you might come across!

What's in 1.100.0 stable

  • Never type
  • Allocator API
  • DropGuard API
  • Conjuring zero-sized types
  • Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo
  • Reducing Cargo cache collisions
  • Cargo min-publish-age
  • Stabilized APIs

Never type

After 10 years and 5 failed stabilization attempts, the never type is finally stable! This also completes the project goal for this work.

The never type, spelled ! in code, is the canonical uninhabited type. It represents the type of diverging computations – computations which never resolve to any value – where any code that follows is unreachable. Expressions that terminate control flow, such as return, break, and std::process::exit, also have the type !.

Since having a value of the never type is impossible, Rust permits a never-to-any coercion, allowing to turn ! into any other type (this is what distinguishes it from any other uninhabited types). This can be used, for example, to not return a value from one of the branches of a match or an if:

fn mrrrow(option: Option<u32>) {
    let value = match option {
        // `x` has type `u32`
        Some(x) => x,
        // `return` has type `!`, which is then coerced to `u32`,
        // allowing the `match` to pass type checking.
        None => return,
    };
    // ...
}

While the never type could already be used and observed this way, and even named in the return type of functions (-> !), this release allows naming the never type anywhere:

fn infallible_unwrap<T>(res: Result<T, !>) -> T {
    // ^^ writing `Result<_, !>` was not allowed before
    let Ok(v) = res;
    v
}

Additionally this release changes Infallible to be an alias to the never type. That makes all old APIs that used Infallible be compatible with using !. This was the plan ever since the introduction of Infallible and is one of the reasons why the never type stabilization was so hard (waffle gave a talk about some of the troubles of the stabilization).

Unfortunately, to allow changing Infallible, we had to introduce a breaking change. This release changes the "never type fallback" from () to ! in editions before 2024 (i.e. 2015, 2018, and 2021), similarly to what has already been done in edition 2024. This should largely be unnoticeable, but can affect code in some rare cases (for example when ignoring a result of a function returning a generic parameter). Note that this change might also make the compiler detect more code as unreachable.

We tried to minimize the impact of this breaking change as much as possible, by providing future compatibility warnings far in advance and releasing fixes to public crates that have been broken by this. If a dependency is failing due to issues with the never type, consider updating it, as a fix might have already been released for it.

Allocator API

This release brings about the stabilization of the core parts of allocator_api, enabling library authors to define custom allocators that can be used together with certain standard library types - currently Vec and Box. These are enabled through the newly-stabilized Allocator trait.

This is the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal. A lot remains to be done still, including expanding the API surface usable with custom allocators and stabilizing their use on more collections and pointer types; with the core trait and design out of the way though, expect to see more being stabilized soon!

DropGuard: run a closure on every exit path

The Drop trait in Rust makes it possible to run code when a variable goes out of scope, regardless of whether we return, ?, or panic. Drop being a part of types means that in Rust you never have to close a socket.

Implementing Drop can however feel a little inconvenient when all you want is to run some code unconditionally when a function exits. This is why we’re introducing core::mem::DropGuard: a new helper type that runs a closure when dropped.

DropGuard takes two arguments: a variable and a closure. It implements Deref and DerefMut so you can keep working with the variable as normal. But when dropped it runs the closure and consumes the variable.

DropGuard also implements a dismiss method which returns the variable from the guard without running the destructor. This makes it possible to quickly implement all-or-nothing transaction-like APIs with a rollback. Here is an example implementing a parser which uses a guard to roll back mutations in case of failure:

use std::mem::DropGuard;
use std::num::ParseIntError;

/// Attempt to parse all `strings` and push them into `nums`.
/// If parsing any of them fails, `nums` remains unchanged.
fn parse_all(nums: &mut Vec<u32>, strings: &[&str]) -> Result<(), ParseIntError> {
    let len = nums.len();
    let mut nums = DropGuard::new(nums, move |nums| {
        nums.truncate(len);    // ← 1. Reset the vec on failure
    });

    for s in strings {
        nums.push(s.parse()?); // ← 2. If `?` returns an error, roll back
    }

    DropGuard::dismiss(nums);  // ← 3. Parsing successful, dismiss the guard
    Ok(())
}

Conjuring zero-sized types

As Rust's unsafe code guidelines are still being decided, it became clear that it would be very useful to decide what exactly it means to create zero-sized types in an unsafe way, and what we should recommend for people to do this.

This question is answered in Rust 1.100 with a single function: std::mem::conjure_zst.

Instead of transmuting (), MaybeUninit::uninit().assume_init(), or various other incantations, this is the dedicated way to create a value of a zero-sized type when you know that doing so is safe to do. If an inhabited type has no size, we know exactly what value it must be: nothing.

Of course, APIs often rely on the inability to construct such types for safety, and that's why this function is unsafe. For example, PyO3's Python<'py> is a zero-sized marker token that represents holding the Python GIL (global interpreter lock). Many of Python's APIs require holding this lock to be safe, but conjuring a token from thin air would allow safe PyO3 calls to violate that precondition.

Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo

Building dependencies that are no longer used or are only needed for specific platforms can slow down builds. Rustc has the unused_crate_dependencies lint for this but it has false positives when used with Cargo because dependencies may be shared between multiple build targets, e.g. dependencies.tracing-subscriber being available for every bin in a package when only some may use it.

Cargo now reports unused dependencies to users, e.g.

warning: unused dependency `tracing-subscriber`
  --> Cargo.toml:23:1
   |
23 | tracing-subscriber.workspace = true
   | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
   |
   = note: `cargo::unused_dependencies` is set to `warn` by default
help: consider removing the dependency on `tracing-subscriber`

A limitation of this warning is that it will only appear when building every build target that may use an entry in a dependencies table. For example, running cargo check --bin foo won't show warnings for unused [dependencies] because another bin may be present that uses them. No warning will be shown for unused dev-dependencies because there isn't a way to ensure every development build target is built.

This warning is being introduced as part of a new linting system for Cargo, controlled by the [lints.cargo] table in Cargo.toml, completing this project goal. See also the other lints that have been introduced.

Reducing Cargo cache collisions

Cargo builds all libraries and binaries in the build-dir and then uplifts final artifacts to the target-dir. At this time, these share a common parent directory. Different build configurations, like --features, can lead to different copies of libraries and binaries in the build-dir. These copies are kept unique by a build-configuration hash but this hash was not always applied due to platform constraints. This can lead to extra rebuilds, missed rebuilds, confusion over what binaries or libraries are used, and so on. These problems get exacerbated when sharing a build-dir across git worktrees.

The build-dir now consistently applies the build-configuration hash to all content by organizing the directories around their build step, rather than their file type, and moving the hash from a file's name to the parent directory.

This work began with the build directory layout project goal in 2025, and its stabilization is a milestone toward a new project goal, unblocking future improvements such as cache garbage collection, cross-workspace cache de-duplication, cross-workspace caching, and fine grain locking.

We previously published a call for testing for the changes that are now taking effect. While this is an internal change, this may break build processes and tests that had workarounds for missing or incomplete features. In some cases, the workaround is no longer needed. See cargo#17287 for possible solutions and to add any new use cases.

Cargo min-publish-age a.k.a. dependency cooldowns

Malicious versions of packages are often caught within hours or days after being published, by either automated scanners or by the community. Rust 1.100 stabilizes Cargo's min-publish-age aware dependency resolution, which lets you wait for that window before it picks up newly published versions. This practice is also known as dependency cooldowns.

You can opt in via .cargo/config.toml:

[registry]
global-min-publish-age = "3 days"

When selecting versions, Cargo now skips any version published more recently than that, and tells you what it held back:

$ cargo update
    Updating crates.io index
     Locking 2 packages to highest compatible version as of min-publish-age
      Adding cc v1.11.0 (available: v1.18.0, published 3 hours ago)
      Adding clap 4.6.7 (available: 4.6.9, published 2 days ago)

When a new version is needed right away, you can override the check for a single update:

$ CARGO_RESOLVER_INCOMPATIBLE_PUBLISH_AGE=allow cargo update clap --precise 4.6.9
    Updating crates.io index
    Updating clap 4.6.7 -> clap 4.6.9 (published 2 days ago, minimum age 3 days)

The newer version will be recorded in Cargo.lock and kept from then on until a later cargo update re-resolves it.

A few things to keep in mind:

  • This depends on the registry recording when each version was published. Versions without a pubtime field in the index are never held back.

  • cargo install ignores the minimum publish age, for both the installed crate and its dependencies. Pin a version with cargo install foo@1.2.3 if needed.

  • Cooldowns reduce the risk from some supply chain attacks but are not a complete defense on their own. Please keep reviewing dependency updates as you otherwise would.

Further work to protect the ecosystem is planned under the crates.io supply chain hardening project goal, including quarantine support and automated detection of suspicious releases.

Stabilized APIs

  • impl PartialEq<Cow<'_, [U]>> for Vec<T, A>
  • impl PartialEq<Cow<'_, [U]>> for &[T]
  • impl PartialEq<Cow<'_, [U]>> for &mut [T]
  • std::alloc::Allocator

  • std::alloc::System

  • impl Allocator for System
  • impl<A: Allocator> Allocator for &A
  • impl<T: Allocator, A: Allocator> Allocator for Box<T, A>
  • impl<A: Allocator> Allocator for &mut A
  • impl<T: Allocator, A: Allocator> Allocator for Arc<T, A>
  • impl<T: Allocator, A: Allocator> Allocator for Rc<T, A>
  • Box::new_in

  • Box::from_non_null_in

  • Box::into_non_null_with_allocator

  • Vec::new_in
  • Vec::with_capacity_in
  • Vec::from_raw_parts_in

  • Vec::into_raw_parts_with_allocator
  • Vec::into_parts_with_allocator
  • Vec::allocator
  • Child::main_thread_handle
  • impl Default for std::sync::Once
  • bool::toggle
  • Box::take
  • Box::map
  • Rc::map
  • Arc::map
  • impl AsRef<T> for !
  • impl AsMut<T> for !
  • core::mem::DropGuard
  • core::mem::conjure_zst
  • UnsafeCell::replace

Other changes

Check out everything that changed in Rust, Cargo, and Clippy.

Contributors to 1.100.0

Many people came together to create Rust 1.100.0. We couldn't have done it without all of you. Thanks!

Language

  • Lint against repeated #[repr(..)] attributes
  • Stabilize extern "custom"
  • Extend dropping_references, dropping_copy_types and undropped_manually_drops lints to drop_in_place

  • Turn the error for repr(align) fields in a repr(packed) type into a deny-by-default lint aligned_fields_in_packed
  • volatile: allow accesses to non-AM memory to trap

Compiler

  • Stabilize -Cprofile-sample-use
  • Enable next solver by default in orphanck

Platform Support

  • i686-pc-windows-gnu is now a tier 2 without host tools target
  • Promote wasm32-wasip3 to Tier 2

Refer to Rust's platform support page for more information on Rust's tiered platform support.

Libraries

  • Stabilize custom allocators
  • Map ENOTSUP to ErrorKind::Unsupported

Stabilized APIs

Cargo

  • Introduced Cargo's own linting system: some Cargo warnings are now emitted as lints that users can control in the [lints.cargo] table. This includes a new built-in unused dependency check via the cargo::unused_dependencies lint. docs #17298
  • Introduced minimum publish age configurations, also known as dependency cooldowns. When the relevant config is set, the resolver ignores versions published more recently than that, unless they are already in Cargo.lock. (RFC 3923) docs #17335
  • cargo-install: now uses the existing lockfile in the .crate tarball by default. --locked in cargo install becomes a no-op. #17388
  • Cargo now uses a new directory layout for intermediate build artifacts. Tools that inspect the build directory may need to use Cargo’s JSON messages to locate build artifacts instead of relying on the build directory layout. The layout is not a stable interface and is subject to change. (build cache doc) #17354

Rustdoc

  • Add new invalid_markdown_table rustdoc lint

Compatibility Notes

  • Closures now more precisely capture variables used in if let. This may cause new errors
  • Check dyn-compatibility of trait objects in more places
  • Infallible is now a type alias to !
  • The never type fallback was changed to ! on all editions
  • box patterns are no longer syntactically allowed
  • Report Query Cycle errors in more cases when computing the layout of enums with explicit discriminants
  • Always escape grapheme extenders in str::escape_debug
  • Make let-else respect macro_rules expr metavariable grouping
  • Iterator::{min,max}(_by_key) changed which Ord methods they use. This cannot change behaviour (other than being potentially faster) for types correctly following the Ord rules, but may impact types with inconsistent trait implementations.
  • Emit an error when trying to enable SSE/AVX on an x86 (32bit or 64bit) softfloat target
  • Require windowed (and exception) for Xtensa ABI
  • windows-gnullvm: always link libunwind statically
  • From version 1.94 up to 1.100 a number of ARMv7-A hardfloat targets required the VFPv3-D32 FPU as a minimum, as they erroneously had the d32 feature in their baseline list of features. Breakage introduced as a result of correcting this can be fixed by passing -Ctarget-feature=+d32 to Rust.
  • Change "Rust" ABI on x86 to use SSE registers if they are always-available for the current target
  • Make the ambiguous_glob_imported_traits lint fire in slightly more cases
  • Make +fix-cortex-a53-835769 a default feature for aarch64-unknown-fuchsia
  • Some impls on Box have been generalised to arbitrary allocators, which may cause new type inference errors
  • The standard library now uses Unicode version 18.0.0
  • WASI SDK version was bumped from 33 to 34
  • On ARM targets, -Ctarget-feature/-Ctarget-cpu values that would alter the ABI are rejected as hard errors now.

Other

  • Test harness now allows passing --test-threads and --color multiple times, with later arguments overriding earlier ones

7:52 PM UTC: We've identified that affected servers are failing automated health checks, which is causing them to become unavailable, and this may be related to a recent change to a component involved in processing those checks. We're testing a configuration change on a subset of affected infrastructure to address this and, if successful, will apply it more broadly. In parallel, we've initiated a restart of all affected servers and are validating whether they're successfully returning to service.

7:30 PM UTC: We're aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact. As a precaution, we've paused all deployments and configuration changes while we review recent changes for any correlation to this event. We've determined that the elevated load isn't driven by an overall increase in traffic, but by a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable, which is shifting load onto the remaining infrastructure. We're investigating what's causing these servers to become unavailable while we work to safely return them to service.

7:16 PM UTC: We're aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact. As a precaution, we've paused all deployments and configuration changes while we review recent changes for any correlation to this event. We've also moved traffic for some services off the affected infrastructure to further reduce load, with additional traffic moves in progress.

6:59 PM UTC: We've completed redistributing connection traffic across our worldwide infrastructure, and we're moving additional traffic off the affected infrastructure to further reduce load. We're also restarting affected servers to return them to service. > Isn't this the company that is trying to get rid of 25% of their employees?

Just clarifying this in general, when a company makes a voluntary offer to some segment of employees, especially at this size, it is a statistics game of how many people accept the buy out.

They did not make the offer to 25% of the employees to downsize by 25%, they did it to downsize by 5% (or something like that), and then made the offer based on how many they expect to accept. This is specifically covered in this line of the geekwire article:

> Microsoft didn’t provide a projection for how many employees will accept, but the company told GeekWire it anticipates a much smaller share than the roughly 30% who took its earlier voluntary retirement offer, which went to longtime employees more likely to take the deal.

They probably expect 10-20% of those offered to take it, which would result in a 2.5-5% total downsizing.


Why do they offer these buy outs at all, doesn't the US have at will employment?

Or is this just a gesture of goodwill to avoid people jumping the ship on their own?


I think both parties probably benefit; people who are more likely to take the offer are those who have another reason to leave (unfulfilled, etc). This will benefit the company in the long run because they can eventually replace them with someone who want to join (people applying for the job).

People who aren't motivated and/or don't back themselves to get another job will stay (i.e. probably the people you want to get rid of)


If you lay people off, you’re on the hook for their unemployment. A voluntary buyout avoids that, and also avoids mandatory reporting for layoffs.


A layoff of any real size has negative impacts to their unemployment insurance premiums and restricts their ability to file PERM for employees. Meeting those targets with voluntary separation prevents those impacts.


You can at will fire but that doesnt stop lawsuits. Most of these require signing docs to get the payout. It is a way to cut cleanly and derisk the cut

Singapore Says U.S. Not Helpful on Investigation Into Suspected Spy’s Company

In a statement, Singapore said it held Alice Huang’s passport months after President Trump was briefed that she was a spy.

Nov. 12, 2026Updated 2:19 p.m. ET

Singapore’s government said on Thursday the United States had provided little help in its investigation into Alice Huang, the woman at the center of a spy plot that has led to the investigation of Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang.

Singaporean authorities held Ms. Huang’s passport to prevent her from leaving the country from June 2025 until February over “potential false declarations” in relation to her company, Megaspeed, which is based in the country, the government said in a statement. She was ultimately released with a “stern warning” and barred from re-entering Singapore.

The statement raises new questions about the response of the Trump administration to the case and why the U.S. government did not more forcefully intervene. According to the timeline in the statement, Singaporean authorities had been holding Ms. Huang’s passport well after President Trump was briefed last fall about her relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive and the belief that she was a Chinese intelligence asset.

The New York Times has reported that Taiwan began monitoring Ms. Huang in 2024 at the guidance of the U.S. government.

In its statement, Singapore said that it had sought information from an American server maker and close Nvidia business partner, Supermicro, but that the company had provided “limited cooperation.” Supermicro, a firm that packages Nvidia’s A.I. chips onto servers that can be used in data centers, has been at the center of a number of chip smuggling investigations across the globe.

Supermicro was a supplier to Megaspeed, a company incorporated in Singapore and run by Ms. Huang, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.

Singapore said in the statement its authorities raised Supermicro’s “limited cooperation” with the U.S. Department of Justice and Federal Bureau of Investigation in July 2025 and “requested their assistance in securing the company’s cooperation.”

“Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company,” the statement said.

Supermicro denied that Megaspeed had ever been a customer. “Supermicro did not sell any products to Megaspeed and has operated in compliance with all applicable U.S. export and re-export control laws,” the company said in a statement.

During questioning, Ms. Huang sought to downplay her role in Megaspeed, according to Singapore’s statement. She was ultimately released because of “insufficient evidence relating to the possible inaccurate declarations for which Megaspeed was being investigated.”

She was issued a “stern warning” and barred from re-entering Singapore. The country’s police are continuing to investigate Megaspeed.

Stitch types

Type What it does Works on
Fill (tatami) Staggered rows, any angle, with underlay (edge walk + rows) and pull compensation Filled shapes
Satin Zigzag column between two rails, with center/contour/zigzag underlay, pull compensation and short stitches on tight curves; plain, S-stitch or zig-zag top stitching; several threads across the column (multicolor satin) Strokes (any width); Ink/Stitch-style two-rail paths with rungs; filled shapes: rings use inner/outer outline, bars/letters/crescents split at their tips (auto-satin), or border follows the outline
Run Running stitch, single or triple (bean) Strokes and outlines
Contour Rows that follow the outline inward, or one spiral out from the center (Ink/Stitch's circular fill) Filled shapes
Blanket E-stitch: a line with prongs into the shape Edges, appliqué
Appliqué Placement line → stop → tack-down → stop → satin cover Filled shapes
Manual Every path point is a needle point Imported machine files, pen tool
Meander One wandering line through the shape, quilting style: light and soft Filled shapes
Ripple Open running-stitch rows following the outline, or one spiral Filled shapes
Cross-stitch A grid of X's, sewn as rows of half-crosses out and back Filled shapes
Tartan Woven stripes in several threads (a mirrored sett you edit in the panel), each thread its own color block Filled shapes

Satins wider than 7 mm are auto-split (shorter, staggered stitches) and use auto spacing (narrow columns more open, wide ones denser).

Planner features:

  • Remove overlaps: fill hidden under later objects isn't sewn (keeps 0.5 mm of overlap).
  • Cap order: center-out, bottom-up, grouped by color, still respecting layering.
  • Routing: travel stitches stay inside shapes: straight across where a straight line stays inside, otherwise round the inside of the outline (Ink/Stitch's underpath), so a fill with a cut-out is sewn with few or no cuts. Trims only where neither works (up to 50 mm of travel).
  • Sewing control per object: a start and an end point (where the thread comes in and leaves, so the next object is close), trim after, stop after (to lay foam or trim appliqué). The document can also connect objects up to N mm apart with running stitches instead of cuts.
  • Fabric presets: standard, thin cotton cap, structured cap, knit.
  • Checks: narrow fills, wide/narrow satins, small lettering, tiny gaps, fully covered objects, hoop fit.
  • Group colors: reorder to cut thread changes without breaking layering.

Mac app

On a Mac with Rust and the Xcode command line tools (xcode-select --install):

packaging/macos/make-app.sh --install    # builds ZigZag.app and copies it to /Applications
packaging/macos/make-app.sh --dmg        # also makes dist/ZigZag-<version>.dmg to share
packaging/macos/make-app.sh --universal  # one app for Apple Silicon and Intel Macs
packaging/macos/make-app.sh --release    # the DMG to publish: universal, signed, notarized

--release signs with your Developer ID and has Apple notarize the app and the DMG, so it opens on any Mac without warnings. Once, beforehand: add a Developer ID Application certificate (Xcode › Settings › Accounts › Manage Certificates › +), make an app-specific password at account.apple.com, and save the notarization credentials in your keychain:

xcrun notarytool store-credentials zigzag-notary --apple-id YOUR_APPLE_ID --team-id YOUR_TEAM_ID

The app bundles the studio, the zigzag command-line tool and the MCP bridge. To use the command line from anywhere: ln -s /Applications/ZigZag.app/Contents/MacOS/zigzag /usr/local/bin/zigzag. For Claude Desktop, point the MCP config at /Applications/ZigZag.app/Contents/MacOS/zigzag-mcp.

Without --release the app is signed ad hoc, not notarized. It opens normally on the Mac that built it. On another Mac, macOS blocks it the first time: open System Settings › Privacy & Security and click Open Anyway (on macOS 14 and earlier, right-click the app and choose Open instead). macOS asks for Bluetooth permission the first time you send to the Skitch.

Agents (MCP)

The studio runs an MCP server on http://127.0.0.1:7878/mcp (Streamable HTTP, localhost only, Origin-checked). Agents edit the live document you're looking at (the tab in front), and every call is one undo step.

MCP in the status bar (bottom right, next to the Skitch) shows whether agents can reach the studio: a gray dot while it waits, green once a client has connected, blue and pulsing while calls come in, red if the server couldn't start. Click it for the address, the commands to connect Claude Code and Claude Desktop (with Copy buttons), the clients that have connected, the recent tool calls (failed ones in red, with the error on hover) and the tools on offer.

Claude Code:

claude mcp add --transport http zigzag http://127.0.0.1:7878/mcp

Claude Desktop / stdio clients (claude_desktop_config.json):

{ "mcpServers": { "zigzag": { "command": "/path/to/zigzag-mcp" } } }

zigzag-mcp forwards to the running studio. Use --port N if you changed it. With "args": ["--headless"] it works without the app open: the same tools on a document no one is watching (zigzag-studio --mcp-stdio), kept only when the agent saves or exports it.

Tools:

  • get_design, add_svg (place/scale artwork in mm), set_object, delete_object, move_object
  • transform_objects (size, scale, rotate, mirror, move), duplicate_objects
  • add_text, edit_text, list_fonts
  • set_document (fabric, hoop, overlaps, cap order, preview color), group_colors
  • render_preview (returns a PNG of the stitches), check_design, get_svg, select
  • open_file (SVG, machine file or image, in a tab of its own), list_documents, switch_document, new_document, undo, save, export (machine formats or html worksheet), send_to_skitch, machine_status

Skitch over Bluetooth

The Skitch window (the toolbar's Send button or File › Send to Skitch…) runs the whole job, like a slicer's device page follows a print: the design on the left, what to do on the right, and the steps across the top (Connect · Home · Send · Trial · Sew · Done).

  • Connect and pair. It scans for the Skitch. The first time, hold the Skitch's Bluetooth button until it beeps, then Connect (or Try Again); if the computer asks to pair, accept. On a Mac the Skitch never appears in System Settings › Bluetooth (it's a Bluetooth LE device): it pairs when ZigZag connects. Allow ZigZag to use Bluetooth if macOS asks (Privacy & Security › Bluetooth). Close Artspira first: the Skitch talks to one app at a time.
  • Home. A machine just turned on asks to be homed (frame off, Accept, frame back on); the window shows the steps and moves on when it's done.
  • Send: the hoop with the design where it will sew: As Placed (where it sits in the studio's hoop, so you can put it high on a cap) or Centered; the threads to have ready, in sewing order, by Brother Embroidery name and number; a "before you sew" checklist; Send Design.
  • Trial run (Brother's name for it; on by default after sending): press Accept on the machine and the needle goes around the design's outline without sewing, so you can check it clears the frame's magnets, seams and the brim. Trial Again whenever you rehoop.
  • Sew: Start, then press Start on the machine. The picture shows what's sewn, faded where it hasn't been yet, with the needle and the thread on now; under it, a timeline of the threads with the needle's place. The side shows progress, time left, the thread on now and the next one, and at each thread change exactly which thread to put on. The canvas and the status bar follow along too.
  • Start / Pause / Stop. Start (or Resume, or Sew Again) readies the machine; Pause is the Skitch's own Start/Stop button (it can't be paused over Bluetooth); Stop ends the job, taking the design off the machine. While paused, drag along the timeline or step the needle by 1, 10 or 100 stitches or back to the thread's start, then Resume.
  • Errors say what they are and what to do (thread breaks, bobbin, needle plate, frame). After a thread break the needle goes back over the gap (6 stitches for the top thread, 2 for the bobbin, as Artspira does).
  • Minimize it (–) to keep working while it stitches: the canvas is your design again, and the machine's icon at the right of the status bar shows what it's doing and how far, with a small bar (click it to bring the window back). The window comes back by itself when the machine needs you: a thread change, an error, or the end.
  • The ••• menu also links to Brother's Skitch how-to videos (threading, the bobbin, the frame, a thread break, tension, cleaning).
  • The window's ••• menu can connect to a simulated machine, which does each step on the machine by itself, to try it all without a Skitch.

Agents can send_to_skitch and follow along with machine_status. The protocol was reverse-engineered (see NOTICE), so avoid firmware updates.

Working out undocumented commands

Thread tension isn't a Bluetooth setting on the Skitch: it's the tension dial on the machine. Speed is fixed (about 400 stitches a minute). The machine does report a block of settings, and Artspira has a settings screen, so two tools are here for working out what else it can do:

  • Settings bytes (in the Skitch window, under the machine's details): reads the settings block the machine reports. Read it, disconnect, change one setting in Artspira, close Artspira, reconnect and read again: the bytes that changed are marked. Every read is kept in skitch-settings.log beside the panel layout. On the command line: zigzag skitch settings --label "what changed" --log settings.log.
  • zigzag capture FILE lists the Skitch conversation in a Bluetooth recording of Artspira, by command name, with changed settings bytes in [brackets] (--all for the upload and polling too, --raw for every ATT operation). It reads both:
    • iPhone: install Apple's Bluetooth logging profile on the phone (developer.apple.com › Bug Reporting › Profiles and Logs), restart it, plug it into the Mac, and in PacketLogger (Apple's Additional Tools for Xcode) choose File › New iOS Trace; save the trace (.pklg).
    • Android: Developer options › Enable Bluetooth HCI snoop log, then adb bugreport and take btsnoop_hci.log from it.

Writing settings stays out of ZigZag until a layout is known and a write of the machine's own settings, unchanged, reads back the same.

Ink/Stitch parity

Checked against Ink/Stitch's features and tool docs:

Ripple, meander, cross-stitch and tartan fills; S-stitch, zigzag and multicolor satin ✓
Params per object with fabric-aware defaults; start/end commands; trim and stop commands ✓ (Stitch panel's Sewing row)
Auto-route (travel inside fills, underpath along the outline), Jump to Stroke ✓ (document's Connect gaps)
Simulator, stitch plan preview, density map, stacking-order labels ✓
Lettering (system fonts, arcs, text on a path, multi-line, case, scale), thread palettes, Match All, thread kits ✓ (Brother and Janome charts)
Duplicate params, select by type, flip satin direction, test swatches, cleanup, troubleshoot (Issues) ✓
Import stitch files and edit at stitch level; PES/DST/EXP/JEF/VP3/PEC ✓
Gradient fill, guided fill; redwork, cutwork; pre-digitized fonts; 60+ thread brands; PDF print not yet

Hatch parity

Checked against Wilcom Hatch's core feature set:

Hatch ZigZag
Tatami, satin, run/triple run, contour fill, blanket, appliqué, manual stitches ✓
Auto underlay, pull compensation, auto spacing, satin auto-split, short stitches ✓
Fabric settings that set densities and compensation ✓ (4 presets)
Lettering with TrueType fonts, straight, arc and path baselines, typed on the canvas ✓ (system fonts)
Select, move, resize, rotate, mirror, duplicate, copy/paste, align to hoop ✓
Digitize shapes and manual stitches by hand ✓ (pen tool)
Remove overlaps, color sequencing, re-order objects ✓
Stitch player, show needle points, grid, measure ✓
Open and save PES, DST, EXP, JEF, VP3 ✓ (VP3 write only)
Production worksheet ✓ (HTML)
Auto-digitize bitmaps ✓ (Image Trace: flat logos, posterized photos, centre lines)
Built-in embroidery fonts, monogramming, multi-hooping, motif/pattern fills, 3D foam not yet

Status

Verified:

  • 136 library tests, 153 editor/MCP tests (UI interactions via egui_kittest, a full agent workflow, a real HTTP JSON-RPC session, atomic batches, the Skitch flow against a simulated machine), with and without Bluetooth built in, plus the 222 tests of the vendored Image Trace.
  • Every writer (PES, DST, EXP, JEF, VP3) reads back through pyembroidery with identical stitch positions; our readers read pyembroidery-written files.
  • PEN output checked against hand-computed sequences.
  • Studio run on Mesa OpenGL and driven by an agent over MCP.

Not yet run against a real Skitch.

Screenshots and videos

Start the studio with ZIGZAG_CAPTURE=<folder> and ⌃⌥⌘S saves the window as a full-resolution PNG; ⌃⌥⌘R starts and stops recording it. packaging/media/encode.sh <folder>/take-001 demo turns a recording into demo.mp4 and demo.gif (needs ffmpeg).

Credits

PES/PEC/DST layouts and the Brother palette are from pyembroidery (MIT). item.title: Nintendo Takes Down Emulators and Firmware in Massive GitHub DMCA Sweep (215 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.ign.com/articles/nintendo-takes-down-switch-emulators-and-mod-chip-firmware-in-massive-github-dmca-sweep, See on Hacker News

Nintendo has sent four DMCA takedown notices to GitHub targeting two Nintendo Switch emulators, Yuzu and Citron Neo, along with mod chip firmware.

This isn't the first time Nintendo has sent takedown notices to GitHub, and it's not even the first time it's tried to take down Yuzu, but the focus this time around seems to be on firmware for mod chips. This particular firmware had 144 repositories, all of which have been removed by GitHub and replaced by a DMCA takedown notice. Mod chips like Picofly can be soldered onto the Nintendo Switch's mainboard, and can be flashed with this firmware to circumvent Nintendo's copy protection.

GitHub has posted Nintendo's November 6 DMCA notice, which says, "The Nintendo Switch console and video games contain technological protection measures ('TPMs') that permit the Nintendo Switch console to interact only with legitimate Nintendo video game files. This process protects Nintendo’s copyright-protected video games, (...) by preventing users from playing pirated copies of Nintendo’s video games on the Nintendo Switch console and by preventing users from unlawfully copying and playing Nintendo’s video games on unauthorized devices."

A History of Every Nintendo Direct in the Switch Era and Beyond

However, while this takedown has effectively wiped out a ton of repositories with mod chip firmware, it seems like it's still being hosted elsewhere on the site, according to TorrentFreak. It's possible, though, that Nintendo isn't finished yet; back in 2024, Nintendo effectively took down 8,500 copies of Yuzu by issuing a takedown that targeted 12 different mirrors of the emulator.

This particular takedown also comes a few days after emulators were able to run the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on PC, so this could be a sign that Nintendo is winding up its lawyers to crack down on emulation once again.

If anything, emulation is a completely different beast in 2026 than it was even in 2024, thanks to the rise of AI. There's already been a wave of AI-made mashup mods that took over Twitter for a couple of weeks, and led Anthropic to coding in a lock to prevent Claude from outright copying games. Game developers have started cracking down on AI ports of games, too. Just last month Rockstar had to take down a browser version of GTA 5, and Bethesda took down an AI-generated Fallout New York game.

item.title: I'm making LLMs work on small and old devices (213 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/hyperionaidev/smolmaxxing/, See on Hacker News

Every device around you is more capable than it looks. TV boxes, old phones, single-board computers and routers all ship with CPUs, RAM and flash that sit idle most of the day. smolmaxxing is about unlocking that capability: finding the biggest language model each device can really run, then pushing it further with custom kernels, smarter memory use and weight streaming. Every claim is measured on the hardware itself.

Device #1 is a Xiaomi TV Box S (3rd Gen): Amlogic S7D, 4× Cortex-A55 @ 2.5 GHz, 1.9 GB of RAM (about 1 GB usable), eMMC flash, Android 14, no root. On it, this repo runs models from 260 K to 16 B parameters:

  • Qwen3.5-0.8B: 16.8 tok/s (2.2× the stock 7.5; measured in the evening of 11-05, see §17).
  • Qwen3.5-2B: 7.7 tok/s in real chat. The box's speed drifts by ~10 % over a day, so every step is measured back to back: §16 gave +11 %, §17 another +7 %.
  • An 8B mixture-of-experts model (Moon-Beam-8B-A1B): 7.2 tok/s in real chat, its experts paged from flash on demand and prefetched one layer ahead (§19).
  • A dense 1-bit 8B model (Bonsai-8B): 5.2 tok/s in real chat, up from 1.2: fully resident in a "headless" mode plus a lookup-table kernel (§19).
  • A 16B mixture-of-experts model (Ling-mini-2.0): 5.1 tok/s in real chat, coherent over 600-word answers, the same expert pager applied unchanged (§20). Twice Moon-Beam's size, but not better per byte: bigger only helps on this box when the model is also better.
  • A dense 9B model: 0.27 tok/s, streaming most of its weights from flash.

Device #2 is a first-generation iPad Air (2013): Apple A7, 2 cores, NEON without dotprod, 1 GB of RAM, iOS 12.5.7, jailbroken, CPU only. A 13-year-old tablet runs a 1.7B-parameter model at 24-26 tok/s (18-22 in long chats), a 4B one at about 10 tok/s, an 8B mixture of experts at about 3.5 tok/s (5 with half its experts, at a quality cost), and a 16B one at 2.6-4.5 tok/s, with their experts paged from flash, from a chat page in its own Safari. See Results on device #2.

Every step is written up experiment by experiment in EXPERIMENT.md (E1-E160).

Devices

Device Status
Xiaomi TV Box S (3rd Gen): Amlogic S7D, Cortex-A55, 2 GB ✅ done: 260K → 16B parameters, 8B at 5-7 tok/s, 16B at 5 tok/s
iPad Air (2013): Apple A7, 2 cores, 1 GB, iOS 12.5.7, jailbroken (ipad-air/) ✅ running: Bonsai-1.7B (1-bit) at 24-26 tok/s, 18-22 in long chats; Bonsai-4B at about 10 tok/s; Moon-Beam-8B-A1B (MoE) at about 3.5 tok/s; Ling-mini-2.0 (16B MoE) at 2.6-4.5 tok/s; CPU only
More TV boxes, phones, single-board computers, routers… 🔜 coming soon

The techniques aren't tied to one box. The 1-bit lookup-table kernel needs only base NEON, as the iPad shows; any ARM chip with dotprod gets the other kernels; and any Linux or Android device with more model than RAM can use the streaming engine.

Scoreboard

"First run" is the first time each model ran on the box:

  • 0.8B: the stock Q4_K_M file.
  • 2B: the stock file, streamed from flash because it didn't fit in RAM. Its first build that fit ran at 4.8, so from there the gain is ×1.6.
  • 4B: the stock file, which thrashed.
  • 8B dense: the last 0.1 GB streamed from flash.
  • 8B MoE: the first expert-pager run, without routing bias.
  • 9B: streamed.
  • 16B: started on the Moon-Beam recipe, so its gain is small.

On this box, the 2B is the best speed-quality balance. Ling-mini-2.0 shows that bigger isn't automatically better: it is twice Moon-Beam's size, but scores worse per byte and runs slower.

What we built, grouped by the bottleneck it attacks (details and numbers in What's in here):

Bottleneck Innovations Biggest wins

Flash (278 MB/s, 5 items) weight streaming with O_DIRECT, MTP speculation when flash-bound, expert pager, cache-aware routing, pre-gated prefetch 9B +69 %; expert misses 13 % → ~2 %; Moon-Beam 4.4 → 7.2
Output quality (2 items) a long-answer degeneration test, a repeat penalty of 1.15 over 256 tokens degenerate long answers 12/13 → 1/13

Granite 4.0 H 1B was the one model close to the 2B's quality. Rebuilt our way (E62), it runs at 5.29 tok/s, below the 2B's 6.55 at slightly lower quality: it carries about twice the 0.8B's weight bytes per token.

Physics of the box: one process can hold ~0.96 GB before Android starts killing things (~1.15 GB in headless mode, with the launchers and Google services force-stopped), and flash reads top out at 278 MB/s, with a lone ~1 MB random read costing ~6 ms. A model that has to stream X MB per token can never beat 278 / X tokens per second. That, not the CPU, is what limits everything above 2B, and why a mixture-of-experts model, which touches ~1 B of its 8 B weights per token, is the way past it.

10 tok/s at 8 B? Measured, not guessed (E98): Moon-Beam reaches 10.4 tok/s with 2 experts per token, but the text turns to gibberish; the best coherent setting is ~7-8 tok/s. Dense Qwen3-8B is Bonsai-8B at 1 bit, and the smallest Qwen MoE (35B-A3B) touches 3× Moon-Beam's weights per token.

Results on device #2

A 2013 iPad Air: Apple A7, 2 cores, NEON without dotprod, 1 GB of RAM, iOS 12.5.7, jailbroken with Amethyst. Everything runs on the CPU with 2 threads and a 1,024-token context, cross-compiled from a Mac. The write-up is §21 of EXPERIMENT.md, and build steps are in ipad-air/README.md.

What we built on the iPad, grouped by the bottleneck it attacks:

Bottleneck Innovations Biggest wins
Compute (2-core A7, no dotprod, 6 items) a multiplication-free 1-bit kernel, the TV's 1-bit lookup-table kernel ported to base NEON, a lookup-table copy of the tied LM head, row-order attention with pruning (2 or 4 q heads per K head), a one-pass sampler with a 40-entry heap, a Q2_K lookup-table kernel for experts Bonsai-1.7B 2.75 → 3.45 → ~11 → 23.7-25.8 tok/s; sampling 3 → 0.23 ms per token; Moon-Beam 2.94 → 3.06 from the Q2_K kernel alone
Address space and RAM (~1.7 GB mappable, ~700 MB usable, 4 items) an expert pager that maps only the non-expert part (experts-last files), pruned LM heads for bailingmoe2 and bailingmoe3, small batches (-c 512 -b 64), std::filesystem compiled out for iOS 12 8B and 16B MoE models load at all, in 556-625 MB; Bonsai-4B fits
Flash (~260 MB/s, 5 items) uncached pread with 4 readers, reads queued by when they're needed, pre-gated prefetch, cache-aware routing bias, decayed-frequency eviction Moon-Beam 1.6 → 3.5 tok/s at no quality cost; misses 42 % → 38 % from eviction alone
Tooling (5 items) an op profiler with page-fault counts, an expert trace and cache simulator, on-device perplexity (tinyppl), model assembly over HTTP range requests, a bench that kills orphaned runs found the LM head that never reached the fast kernel (45 of 72 ms); ruled out the soft-fault theory; built a 5.5 GB model with 1.4 GB of Mac disk

How Bonsai-1.7B got from 2.75 to about 25 tok/s (same model file throughout):

Step tok/s What changed
Stock llama.cpp, 2 threads 2.75 emulates dotprod with widening multiplies
Multiplication-free NEON kernel 3.45 weights are ±1, so no multiply is needed; output identical
Lookup-table kernel from device #1, ported to base NEON about 11 its dotprod requirement turned out to be only an assumption
The output head on that kernel 18-22 151,669 rows isn't a multiple of 32, so the tied head had never reached it: 45 of 72 ms per token
Row-order attention with pruning, and a sampler that doesn't sort the vocabulary 23.7-25.8 the KV cache stores all heads of a row side by side, so one head at a time missed the cache constantly

In long chats (400-token answers), the three turns went from 15.4 / 7.6 / 8.2 to 21.8 / 17.9 / 18.4 tok/s through the attention work alone. The pruning threshold that holds long chats above 17 costs +0.42 % perplexity at 1,024 tokens of context, near the ±0.3 % noise floor; GGML_FA_EPS=0.0001 trades that back for about 15 tok/s.

An 8B model, through an expert pager. iOS 12 caps a process at about 1.7 GB of mapped address space (1.3 GB for the web server's user), so Moon-Beam-8B's 2.6 GB file can't even be mapped, and keeping fewer experts to make it fit more than doubles its perplexity (§21.7). Dense Bonsai-8B runs at 0.08 tok/s from flash. So the model file is rewritten with its experts last, only the 474 MB before them is mapped, and each layer keeps 14 experts in RAM, reading the others from flash with pread when the router picks them. Results match the unpaged model exactly. A small routing bias toward experts already in RAM (+0.3 % perplexity, inside the noise) brought it to 2.4-2.8 tok/s in about 600 MB (§21.8). Round 2 (§21.9) queues flash reads by when they're needed, prefetches the next layer's likely experts, and runs the experts through a lookup-table kernel for Q2_K: 3.4 tok/s, 40× the dense 8B, at +0.7 % perplexity on the full eval text. The flash is still the limit: each token reads about 53 MB at 266 MB/s. Wiring weights in RAM kernel-panicked the iPad, like a pool of 16 did before. Round 3 (§21.10) evicts by decayed use frequency instead of recency, for 3.5 tok/s at no quality cost. 5 tok/s takes 4 experts per token instead of 8 (+27 % perplexity); choosing the count per token adaptively turned out no better than a fixed count. A 16B model (§21.11): Ling-mini-2.0, 16.3B parameters with 256 small experts per layer, runs through the same pager at 2.6 tok/s with unchanged routing, 3.3 at +2.6 % perplexity and 4.5 with a strong cache bias, in under 580 MB. Its 5.5 GB file was assembled from two published quantizations over HTTP range requests and streamed straight to the iPad, since the Mac had no room for it. It is twice Moon-Beam's size at the same speed, but not a better model (+3 % perplexity).

Limits worth knowing. Bonsai is a 1-bit model and still gets facts wrong (in one test it called Mercury the closest planet to Earth). About 700 MB is the practical memory ceiling: 1-bit weights don't compress, so iOS starts killing processes past it, which is why the 4B needs a 512-token context. The jailbreak doesn't survive a reboot. The fast output head adds 2-3 s to the first prompt after each launch.

What's in here

Kernels for Cortex-A55 (ARMv8.2 dotprod, no i8mm), as a patch on llama.cpp v0.8.0, each with an exactness test against a scalar reference:

Kernel Before → after Where
Q2_K, repacked 8 rows × 4 bytes for vdotq_laneq (upstream repacks Q2_K only on x86 / RISC-V) 7.8 → 13.9 G weights/s; generation +41 %, prompt 2.4× E34
TQ1_0 / TQ2_0 ternary, repacked 9.5 → 14.4 / 11.9 → 19.1 G weights/s E38
Ternary Q2_0 → lossless 1.875 bits/weight in RAM (base-3 packing that keeps the per-64 scales) Ternary-Bonsai-4B from "thrashes" to 3.2 tok/s E39, E42
Q1_0 bit planes: vtst turns a bit plane straight into a mask for vdot, no table lookups; 8-bit row-affine scales (−5.6 %, 0.07 % error) Bonsai-4B 3.02 → 4.22 tok/s; Bonsai-8B fits in 0.96 GB E44, E52
Fused Gated-DeltaNet step with direct state write (Qwen3.5) 2B 6.0 → 6.3-6.7 tok/s E28
DeltaNet state read in place by id instead of a 1 MB/layer gather every token; fp16 state (LLAMA_STATE_F16=1, on by default in the UI) 0.8B 11.9 → 12.9 tok/s; 2B +2.5 % for +0.15 % perplexity E56, E61, E65
The LM head on the fast kernel: the 65,668-row head was never repacked (ggml repacks only row counts divisible by 8), so 4 token rows were added; embedding rows are then rebuilt from the repacked head (inverse 8-row interleave) instead of read from flash; the one-token DeltaNet conv step fused from 4 nodes into one NEON op 2B +7 % (bench and chat); 0.8B +9.5 % E69-E72
Ternary weights in 2-bit fields, with scales merged per 128: on the in-order A55, one base-3 digit costs ~5 NEON ops per 16 weights and a 2-bit field costs 2, so spending 13 % more RAM buys speed. Merging adjacent scales costs +0.18 % perplexity Ternary-Bonsai-4B 3.2 → 4.3 tok/s in chat, prompt 7.0 → 9.6 E76, E77
1-bit lookup-table kernel (Four-Russians / T-MAC style): 32 rows per group, one 16-entry table per 4 activations built straight from the float activations, ~8 NEON ops + 2 loads per 128 multiply-adds vs 16 + 4 Bonsai-8B 3.77 → 5.1-5.4 tok/s (with E82, E88) E81
Q8_0 attention with a threshold: all K dots first with sdot, so the softmax maximum is known up front, then expf and V work skipped for rows below max + ln(1e-4) a 1,000-token answer no longer halves the speed (2.50 → ~4 tok/s at the end) E86
Guided matmul scheduling: each thread grabs remaining / (2 × threads) rows, so a slow or preempted thread leaves a short tail instead of ~28 ms per token of idle cores; single-row element-wise ops split by columns (ggml left them all on thread 0) 2B 6.26 → 6.54 tok/s; 0.8B +1.4 % E63, E64

Memory tricks:

  • Pruned LM head: keep only the ~49-66 K most useful vocabulary rows, chosen by token frequency on English, code and 7 other languages. The other logits are scattered to −inf. Saves 0.2-0.5 GB and misses ~1 % of English tokens.
  • Repack cache on flash (GGML_REPACK_CACHE): repacked weights are written to a file once and mapped afterwards. Models load in seconds.

Headless mode (tools/tv-llm-mode.sh on|off): a small foreground activity, then the launchers, Google services and other heavy apps are force-stopped, and svc power stayon keeps the animated screensaver (17 % of a core) away. Nothing persistent except stay-awake, which off restores. MemAvailable ~1000 → ~1300 MB. A fork-free guard (tools/tv-watch.c) replaced a shell loop that started ~25 processes a second and cost 10 % of the speed.

Expert pager for mixture-of-experts models (ggml-cpu/moe-pager-tv.inc):

  • Experts live on flash: each expert tensor is overlaid with empty anonymous memory, and right after a layer's routing the missing experts are read with parallel O_DIRECT straight into their own addresses; a per-layer LRU pool (43 of 128 experts) keeps the rest. Kernels see an ordinary tensor. The GGUF's own expert bytes are hole-punched once the repack cache holds them, so the model costs one copy of its weights on flash.
  • Cache-aware routing (GGML_MOE_BIAS): a small bonus for experts already in RAM cuts misses from 13 % to ~2 % for a measured quality cost (arXiv 2412.00099 has the idea on other models). Fewer experts per token (LLAMA_MOE_USED=6) is the other dial.
  • Warm start from a list of each layer's most used experts, and pre-gated prefetch: layer L+2's router applied to layer L's hidden state, predicting what the router will actually pick (sigmoid, the model's own selection bias and the cache bonus), loads ~60 % of misses before they are needed.
  • Why answers looped, and the fix: 2-bit experts break long-form coherence after ~250-300 words, and routing bias amplifies it. DRY sampling only hides it (the model paraphrases its loop); a repeat penalty of 1.15 over 256 tokens brings degenerate long answers from 12/13 to 1/13 on the TV (E99, E100).

Weight streaming for models bigger than RAM (ggml-cpu/stream-tv.inc):

  • What stays in RAM: a chosen part of the weights stays resident. The rest lives in "stream zones".
  • Prefetch: a hook on every matmul records the order the weights are used. Reader threads then fetch zone weights ahead of time with parallel 8 MB O_DIRECT reads straight into the weights' own addresses, at the flash's full 278 MB/s.
  • Correctness: every compute thread waits until its weight is completely loaded, so a wrong prediction costs time, never correctness.
  • Drop-behind: each zone weight is freed right after use.
  • Verify mode: GGML_STREAM_VERIFY=1 compares every streamed tensor with the file. It found two silent-corruption bugs, which are fixed and documented in E48 and E50.
  • Speculative decoding: with the model's own MTP head, verifying 2 tokens costs about one pass over the weights when the pass is flash-bound, so it pays off (+69 %). On the in-RAM 2B it lost (E31).

Profiling (env switches in the patch): GGML_OPPROF=1 per-op table, GGML_OPPROF=2 a node-by-node, per-thread trace of one graph (tools/optrace.py), LLAMA_UBATCH_PROF / GGML_CPU_PROF phase timings. They showed where a small model's time really goes (E57): ~71 % Q4_K matmuls, and only ~2 ms per token of barriers and scheduling.

Tooling:

  • Streaming GGUF rewriter: adds a pruned head, extra tensors and metadata in one sequential pass, so Hugging Face → Mac → TV pipelines never store the model on the Mac.
  • MTP fetcher: range-reads only the MTP tensors from safetensors.
  • Memory guard: wraps every heavy run on the TV.
  • Benchmark and perplexity harnesses, a model screener that streams any Hugging Face GGUF to the TV and scores it (tools/screen-small.sh), and a live token-stream web UI.

Quick start

You need: the TV box (or another ARMv8.2 Android device) with network ADB, adb, zig (for static aarch64 musl builds), cmake + ninja, python3, and uv (for numpy).

export ADB_SERIAL=<tv-ip>:5555          # every script talks to the box through this
adb connect $ADB_SERIAL

# 1. llama.cpp v0.8.0 + the patch, cross-compiled for the TV
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp third_party/llama.cpp
cd third_party/llama.cpp && git checkout 8642541 && git apply ../../patches/llama.cpp-v0.8.0-tvbox.patch
cmake -S . -B build-tv -G Ninja -DCMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME=Linux -DCMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR=aarch64 \
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=$PWD/../../zigcc/cc -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=$PWD/../../zigcc/c++ -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS=-static -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF -DGGML_NATIVE=OFF \
  -DGGML_CPU_ARM_ARCH=armv8.2-a+dotprod+fp16 -DGGML_OPENMP=OFF -DLLAMA_OPENSSL=OFF -DLLAMA_BUILD_TESTS=OFF
ninja -C build-tv llama-server llama-cli llama-bench llama-perplexity llama-quantize
cd ../..
adb -s $ADB_SERIAL shell mkdir -p /data/local/tmp/llm/patched25 /data/local/tmp/llm/patched
adb -s $ADB_SERIAL push third_party/llama.cpp/build-tv/bin/llama-{server,cli,bench,perplexity} /data/local/tmp/llm/patched25/
adb -s $ADB_SERIAL push third_party/llama.cpp/build-tv/bin/llama-quantize /data/local/tmp/llm/patched/   # used by tools/tv-quant.sh
zig cc -target aarch64-linux-musl -O2 -static -o gguf_recut tools/gguf-recut/gguf_recut.c && adb -s $ADB_SERIAL push gguf_recut /data/local/tmp/llm/

# 2. models: rebuilt from their Hugging Face sources straight onto the TV (see below)
tools/rebuild-models.sh 2b          # also: 08 4b b8 tb8 q9 mb lm caches

# 3. the live chat page (default: the 2B on patched25 with fp16 state), then open http://<tv-ip>:8090 from any device on the network
tv-llm-ui/start.sh
tv-llm-ui/start.sh stop

Other models:

# Moon-Beam-8B-A1B MoE, ~7.2 tok/s (first: `tools/rebuild-models.sh mb`, needs a native Mac build and ~9 GB on the Mac while it runs).
# start.sh turns on headless mode, the expert pager, routing bias, prefetch and the repeat penalty; POOL / BIAS / EXPERTS override them.
MODEL=mb-q2-h60.gguf tv-llm-ui/start.sh
# Ling-mini-2.0 16B MoE, ~5.1 tok/s (first: `tools/rebuild-models.sh lm`)
MODEL=lm2-q2-h60.gguf tv-llm-ui/start.sh
# Bonsai-8B 1-bit fully resident, ~5.2 tok/s (first: `tools/rebuild-models.sh b8`; the repack cache is written on first start)
MODEL=b8-q1-hml.gguf tv-llm-ui/start.sh
sh /data/local/tmp/llm/tv-llm-mode.sh off   # on the TV, afterwards: launcher and screensaver back
# Qwen3.5-0.8B, ~16 tok/s (first: `tools/rebuild-models.sh 08`, needs a native Mac build of llama-quantize)
MODEL=q08-q4k-h65p8.gguf tv-llm-ui/start.sh
# The 8B / 9B numbers below were measured with the build of that time (patched16); the current build has the same
# code plus §15-17. GGML_CHUNK_GUIDED=0 in SENV restores the old matmul scheduling. No fp16 state with MTP.
# Bonsai-8B 1-bit with streaming and no headless mode, ~1.2 tok/s (first run: `tools/rebuild-models.sh b8 caches`)
MODEL=b8-q1-hml.gguf BIN=patched25 EXTRA="-ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 -fa on -cram 0" \
  SENV="GGML_REPACK_CACHE=/data/local/tmp/llm/cache/b8c GGML_REPACK_RESIDENT_MB=800 GGML_STREAM_MODE=cache GGML_STREAM_WINDOW_MB=64" tv-llm-ui/start.sh
# Qwen3.5-9B with MTP, ~0.27 tok/s
MODEL=q9-iq2-h65-mtp.gguf BIN=patched25 EXTRA="-nr -ctxcp 0 -cram 0 -ub 16 -b 64 --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 1" \
  SENV="LLAMA_STREAM_RESIDENT_MB=600 LLAMA_STREAM_PIN=output.,blk.32. GGML_STREAM_WINDOW_MB=64" tv-llm-ui/start.sh

Everything on the box lives in /data/local/tmp/llm and runs as the adb shell user. The only system setting touched is stay-awake in headless mode (svc power stayon), which tv-llm-mode.sh off turns back off. adb shell rm -rf /data/local/tmp/llm removes it all.

Model files: not in git, rebuildable

The model files (0.5-4 GB each) are not in this repo. tools/rebuild-models.sh recreates every one from public Hugging Face files, streaming them through tools/gguf_build.py onto the TV. The SHA-256s below are of the files used in the experiments. Rebuilds of the 4B, Bonsai-8B and 9B files were checked byte-identical.

Layout

Path What

patches/llama.cpp-v0.8.0-tvbox.patch every change to llama.cpp: pruned head (output_ids) for Qwen3 / Qwen3.5 / Granite 4.0 H, the kernels above (ggml-cpu/repack-*-tv.inc), fused DeltaNet (state read by id, optional fp16 state, one-token conv step), the 1-bit LUT kernel, Q8_0 attention, the MoE expert pager with routing bias and prefetch (ggml-cpu/moe-pager-tv.inc), a pruned head for bailingmoe3, embedding rows from the resident head, repack cache and streaming engine (ggml-cpu/stream-tv.inc, loader hooks), padded small batches, op profiler, pruned-head-aware perplexity, Vulkan tuning for Mali
tools/ GGUF rewriter / head pruner / re-cutter, vocabulary selection, corpus and MTP fetchers, model rebuild script, TV memory guard and RAM helper, benchmark sweeps, kernel benches and exactness checks (kbench/), flash benchmark
tv-llm-ui/ the live token-stream page for llama-server (confidence colours, top-3 alternatives, speed, box stats), its launcher and the benchmark harness
tiny-llm-web/ the llama2.c story server + TV page from the first experiment
bench/ results.jsonl (every chat benchmark: prompts, outputs, speeds) and raw/ (logs of every experiment)
data/ head-id lists and the two evaluation texts
zigcc/ zig wrappers for cross-compiling static aarch64 binaries
ipad-air/ device #2: cross-compile for iOS 12, smolchat (terminal chat and Safari web page), deploy and benchmark scripts (README, §21)
screenshots/ the web pages running on the TV

Lessons

  • On this box the 2B at 4 bits beats every bigger model at 1-2 bits. Post-training quantization below ~2.5 bits breaks normal models (E22, E23, E35). Models trained for 1-bit or ternary hold up, but at 4-8 B they don't fit without streaming.
  • Past RAM, flash bandwidth sets the speed. The kernel's LRU is the worst possible policy for a cyclic scan bigger than the cache: it re-reads everything every token. Keep a fixed resident set and stream the rest yourself.
  • Batching is free when you are flash-bound. Prompts and speculative verification cost about one weight pass, whatever their size.
  • Measure, then verify. Two streaming bugs gave plausible speeds and wrong numbers; only comparing tensors with the file, and perplexity with a Mac reference, caught them.
  • Small models are mostly vocabulary. Qwen3.5-0.8B's 248K-row head is a third of its weights; pruning it to 65K rows plus all-Q4_K took it from 7.5 to 12.1 tok/s (E55). Small models also lose more to 4 bits (+7 % perplexity vs +2.3 % for the 2B).
  • Simulate before you write a kernel. Activation sparsity (E58) and a low-rank head (E60) both looked promising on paper; a quality simulation on the Mac killed each in under an hour.
  • On an in-order core, count NEON ops as well as bytes. Tighter packing saved 20 % of the bytes and cost 2.5× the ops; undoing it made the 4B 33 % faster in chat (E76, E77). The 4-bit kernel is the opposite case, limited by RAM (E27), so the trick does not help the 2B or 0.8B.
  • Check that every big matrix reaches the fast kernel. The 2B's head (65,668 rows, ~10 % of each token's weights) silently ran on the generic kernel for weeks because ggml only repacks row counts divisible by 8; four extra rows gave +5.8 % (E71, E72). The load log's repack buffer size gives it away.
  • Most of the RAM was Android's, not the model's. Force-stopping the launchers and Google services for the duration (nothing persistent) let Bonsai-8B sit fully in RAM: 1.2 → 3.6 tok/s before any kernel work (E80). An animated screensaver and a guard that forked 25 times a second each cost another 10-15 % (E82, E88).
  • For a mixture-of-experts model the flash is a cache miss, not a stream. A ~6 ms miss per expert means the pool hit rate decides the speed; routing toward cached experts and prefetching what the next router will pick turned 4.4 into 7.2 tok/s.
  • Perplexity can't see loops. It scores one token at a time on clean text; the 2-bit model scored fine and still fell into loops in 12 of 13 long answers. Score long free-running generations too (tools/loop_stats.py), and compare models with different tokenizers in bits per byte, never in perplexity.
  • Past 9B, count resident bytes, not parameters. The ceiling for a mixture-of-experts model here is the non-expert weights that must stay in RAM plus a useful expert pool. Ling-mini-2.0 (16B) keeps 279 MB resident and runs at 5 tok/s; Qwen3.6-35B-A3B would need ~870 MB before caching a single expert (§20).
  • Guard the box. After two early kernel panics, every heavy run goes through a wrapper that kills it below 180 MB of free memory.

License

MIT. The llama.cpp patch is a derivative of llama.cpp (MIT). Model weights keep their own licenses, and the evaluation texts are Wikipedia excerpts (CC BY-SA 4.0).

item.title: Talking Zen 6 with Mike Clark at AMD In-Depth (153 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://chipsandcheese.com/p/talking-zen-6-with-mike-clark-at, See on Hacker News

Hello you fine Internet folks,

I sat down with AMD’s Mike Clark to talk about Zen 6, the evolution from Zen 5 and what some of the differences are between Zen 6 and Zen 6c and what drove some of those changes.

Hope y’all enjoy!

The transcript below has been edited for readability and conciseness.

George Cozma: Hello, you fine Internet folks. We’re here at AMD In-Depth, where we’re talking about Venice. With me, I have a returning guest, Mike Clark. Would you like to tell the audience who you are?

Mike Clark: Hi, I’m Mike Clark, the original architect of Zen. Some people refer to me as “Zen Daddy.” I’ve been working on cores here at AMD for 33 years, and we’ve got another great one coming, so I’m very proud of the design team I get to represent here today.

George Cozma: I’ve had some hands-on time with Zen 6c. Let’s talk about the change that’s happened with Zen 6 and Zen 6c, what I refer to in my piece as the Zen 6 family. Why is it different from previous generations?

Mike Clark: Right. Starting with Zen 4, we’ve been going through this evolution of having two core families. Before, we were really just using the denser technology as an area play. In this generation, having learned a lot, as we were filling out that denser version of the core, we wanted to leverage it to add some extra IPC within the core. So if you look more in-depth at what we have, what used to be our classic design, we now think of as our high-frequency design. And our dense technology is now our top-of-the-line, no-questions-asked performance core, because we’ve also enabled the full L3 in that implementation, at 4MB per core. So we have 32 of those cores, 128MB of L3, and the highest IPC you can get in that core.

George Cozma: Awesome. So far, one thing I’ve noticed is that the vector scheduler is a bit bigger on Zen 6c. What was the reasoning for increasing that on Zen 6c?

Mike Clark: Well, that wasn’t the only thing we increased. One principle we follow is that we don’t want to create a delta between the two architectures that software has to be optimized for. We want them to have the same fit and feel, so the same optimizations apply to both. But because of its reduced frequency target, Zen 6c can have a little more capacity in the queues, since it doesn’t have to reach the maximum frequency the high-frequency core has to hit. The floating-point scheduler is just one example. There are other queues throughout the core that are larger in Zen 6c, to pull out a little more IPC and get a little more leverage in that SMT environment as well.

George Cozma: Interesting. Both Zen 6 and Zen 6c build on the design you had in Zen 5, and one of the interesting things with Zen 5 was the dual decode setup. Has the front end changed much to let a single thread make better use of both decode clusters?

Mike Clark: Yes. As you said, Zen 5 was a new foundation, with the ability to fetch two basic blocks and get them down the line. But it gets quite complicated with one thread running larger-footprint workloads, where some of it might be hitting the I-cache and some of it might be hitting the op cache, and you’re trying to get everything synced up. So we spent a lot of time optimizing that and making it more efficient from both a delivery and a power perspective: less power wasted, and more efficient delivery from that new front end.

George Cozma: Awesome. Going down into the execution engine, I also noticed that the number of integer multiply units has gone down from three to two. Could you talk a bit about what drove that choice?

Mike Clark: It really came out of the Zen 5 design, where we had a more unified scheduler. To make a scheduler simpler, you want the units it schedules into to be very uniform, and the way we had set up those schedulers, adding a third multiplier to the group it was scheduling into was easy and didn’t add complication. In Zen 6, we realized that to really scale out the architecture, we needed to go back to more distributed schedulers, which now schedule into the ALUs. We hadn’t seen much uptick from that extra multiplier on Zen 5, so to optimize the area and the schedulers, we went back to two multipliers.

George Cozma: Speaking of integer multiply, on the vector side you’ve added two more VNNI units. What was the impetus for adding them, and at what point in the design did you add them?

Mike Clark: As I said in the talk, these are long design programs. We weren’t designing Zen 6 to be an agentic core. When we started, no one was really even using that term. But Zen 5 was a whole new foundation for AI workloads, and we’ve always believed the core has a place in AI: orchestration, data type manipulation, smaller models. So we were always focused on making the core good at AI. It’s not going to beat a GPU, and that’s not the point. We realized we probably should have some more VNNI, given where we were seeing inference go, and the team rallied around that. It was kind of late, since these are long-lead projects and the floor plan was set, but the team rallied, we were able to squeeze a couple more VNNI pipes in there, and it was a big success.

George Cozma: Again on the vector side, one of the oddities of Zen 5 was that although the wires were all there, the load unit could only do two vector loads at a time. What changed within the Zen 6 core to allow four vector loads, assuming they’re either 128 or 256 bits?

Mike Clark: We can do the 256-bit loads. Since we were able to do two 512-bit loads, we already had 1,024 wires headed over there. Obviously, using them piecemeal versus as one contiguous set complicates the design. I think it’s something we always wanted to do on Zen 5, but with all the change and getting it working, we left that for the Zen 6 team, and they were awesome. We’re all really one team at AMD anyway, and sometimes things intersect at different points in the roadmap. This was the time to do it.

George Cozma: Speaking of bandwidth into the caches, the L2 in Zen 5 had some oddities where it couldn’t always hit 64 bytes per cycle on reads. What changed in Zen 6 to allow that? Because I’ve been able to measure it, and it does hit that.

Mike Clark: Honestly, sometimes you just don’t see some of these things. A lot of it was that we would be over-prefetching, and prefetches that hit in the L2 would be robbing L2 bandwidth. So we made sure we could sustain those prefetches alongside demand requests, reduce the conflicts, and deliver the full 64 bytes per cycle that we want.

George Cozma: Awesome. Circling all the way back to the front: the all-important branch predictor. There seems to have been a reduction in branch misprediction latency, so when you miss a branch, the number of cycles it takes to recover has gone down. What I also noticed, which is really neat, is that there wasn’t any reduction in accuracy. So how did you pull off not only a faster branch predictor, but one that’s even slightly more accurate than Zen 5’s already very accurate predictor?

Mike Clark: The branch prediction team, as you know, is very algorithmic. There’s lots of design space and lots of exploration, and AI has even been getting involved in helping us figure out how to optimize it. It’s a great optimization problem: the number of TAGE tables, how much information they hold, accuracy. So we set out to make a more efficient one. That was an area where we didn’t really want to grow; we thought we could be more efficient in the way we lay out the tables for prediction. And we’re always focused on our pipeline length. No matter how good a branch predictor you build, there are always hard-to-predict branches, and you’re always going to mispredict. So each generation, we’re monomaniacally focused on getting going again as fast as we can when we’re wrong. There are lots of unique tricks we pull to get that redirect back into the front end and get it flowing as fast as possible. And you’ve observed it, which is great.

George Cozma: Yeah. I haven’t had time on Zen 6 yet, but I have had time on Zen 6c, and in SPECint 2026 it matches your fastest Zen 5 server CPU. That’s very impressive, especially considering the clock deficit. Wrapping this all up and moving outside the core into the L3, there are obviously topology differences between the 12-core and 32-core CCDs. How much were you able to mitigate those differences inside the core, building up structures to tolerate latency, to compensate for the slightly increased L3 latency?

Mike Clark: As I always talk about, the design has to be balanced. As we grow the capacity of a structure, the new technology helps it shrink, so the physical distance doesn’t grow linearly, but unfortunately the distance does grow. Inside the L3, there are a lot of tricks I can’t talk about...

George Cozma: The secret sauce!

Mike Clark: [In order to] maintain bandwidth within the L3 mesh so we can keep delivering to the cores. And in the cores, we do grow the queues to handle those higher latencies.

George Cozma: Awesome. My penultimate question: Verano is adding LPDDR5X to the EPYC ecosystem. Were there any design considerations between LPDDR5X and DDR5 that you had to think about when designing the core?

Mike Clark: At the CCX level, we focus a lot on bandwidth per core. I think Mahesh talked a lot about the SDP ports, with 32-byte reads per port, so we try to make sure we have enough bandwidth between the CCD and the IOD. But we were already well provisioned for bandwidth with MRDIMMs, so that construction, the winglets and choosing a different memory technology, didn’t really have a major impact on how we built the core.

George Cozma: Awesome. Usually this is where I’d ask what your favorite type of cheese is, but since we already know that: have you tried any new cheeses lately?

Mike Clark: I have. My new favorite is Cotija cheese.

George Cozma: Oh!

Mike Clark: I’ve been eating a lot of tacos.

George Cozma: You’ve got to love Cotija on tacos. It’s absolutely amazing. Well, thank you so much for sitting down with me. If you like videos like this, hit like and subscribe; it does help with the algorithm. There are PayPal and Patreon links in the description, as well as a transcript of this on the Chips and Cheese website. Thank you so much.

Mike Clark: Thanks for having me, George. I always look forward to coming and talking with you about what this awesome AMD CPU design team has created, and you always have so many good questions. I wish I could answer more, since we do have to protect our secret sauce, but I really enjoy helping you understand some of our thought processes, the challenges we face, and how we’ve been able to overcome them.

George Cozma: Well, it’s always fun to sit down with you and talk, not just about what you’re doing, but also what the team is doing and what you’re looking forward to in the future. So thank you so much.

Mike Clark: Thank you.

George Cozma: I’ll see you in the next one. Have a good one, folks!
