In a follow up to his famous article, No Silver Bullet30:, where he argued that we won’t ever see another order-of-magnitude increase in programmer productivity31, Fred Brooks writes:

Is Einstein’s statement that nothing can travel faster than the speed of light “bleak” or “gloomy?” How about Gödel’s result that some things cannot be computed? … [T]he very nature of software makes it unlikely that there will ever be any silver bullets32.

He then quotes Wladyslaw M. Turski, and his take on No Siver Bullet:

Of all misguided scientific endeavours, none are more pathetic than the search for the philosophers’ stone, a substance supposed to change base metals into gold. The supreme object of alchemy, ardently pursued by generations of researchers generously funded by secular and spiritual rulers, is an undiluted extract of wishful thinking, of the common assumption that things are as we would like them to be. It is a very human belief. It takes a lot of effort to accept the existence of insoluble problems. The wish to see a way out, against all odds, even when it is proven that it does not exist, is very, very strong. And most of us have a lot of sympathy for these courageous souls who try to achieve the impossible. And so it continues. Dissertations on squaring a circle are being written. Lotions to restore lost hair are concocted and sell well. Methods to improve software productivity are hatched and sell very well. All too often we are inclined to follow our own optimism (or exploit the optimistic hopes of our sponsors). All too often we are willing to disregard the voice of reason and heed the siren calls of panacea pushers.

I believe that everything we’ve covered in the first two sections is a mathematical proof that Brooks and Turski are right. But what are we to do?

A Call for Empiricism

We’ve seen that computer science studies objects —- computer programs —- that are composed of very basic components, be they beta reductions in lambda calculus or Turing machine instructions, that are easily subject to full mathematical reasoning on their own, but their interaction is essentially intractable. I think this is similar to physics, where, for example, the gravity equation is very simple, and the equation composes beautifully for multiple instances, and yet even the interaction of three bodies is already chaotic and has no closed form.

I think we should take a page out of physics’s book, and embrace empiricism. Let’s consider the verification problem again:

We must restrict either the left hand side or the right hand side. I hope it’s clear by now that it’s unlikely we’ll find a general useful category of programs for which verification is affordable, as verifying even the most simple computational model, the FSM, is in general also infeasible. But we can make the following obvious observation: all programs we care about are created by people. If you like, we can consider humanity to be one large TM that generates all machines $M$. It is likely that patterns could be found in the machines humanity generates that would allow some affordable verification. But because analyzing humanity as a program is truly infeasible, the only viable method is empirical study of the programs humans write. We can begin with a taxonomy of program types, size, cost, etc.

This observation also makes some useful restrictions of the right side possible. So far even the simplest properties we considered (like halting) were global ones. But in practice we know —- empirically! —- that some local properties are also very useful to prove. A great example of that is memory safety, which is known to be a source of common and costly bugs. We may be able to find other useful local properties, but this, too, would require empirical study. A great place to start would be a taxonomy of bugs by cause, prevalence, association with program types, and, most importantly – cost.

Such empirical studies would require the cooperation of academia and industry. With that empirical knowledge in hand, we’ll be able to tackle the interesting special cases using ad-hoc mathematical techniques, just as physics does: simplifying assumptions, heuristics, or approximations.

One such beautiful example of empirical research is a recent study at the university of Toronto, that discovered that a vast majority of catastrophic failures in large distributed system is due to programmers not putting enough thought into error-handling code. This is clearly a psychological effect.

Almost all (92%) of the catastrophic system failures are the result of incorrect handling of non-fatal errors explicitly signaled in software in 58% of the catastrophic failures, the underlying faults could easily have been detected through simple testing of error handling code33.

They studied catastrophic failures in distributed systems, and discovered that a large number of errors is a result of people not putting any thought into exception-handling code. This is clearly a psychological phenomenon of humans writing software. The researchers then created a simple linter that identifies this dangerous pattern. The simple tool would have prevented 33% of all catastrophic failures in Cassandra, HBase, HDFS, and MapReduce.

Computer science isn’t physics, but it isn’t math, either. Juris Hartmanis writes:

Computer science differs from the known sciences so deeply that it has to be viewed as a new species among the sciences34.

Complexity is Essential!

I’ll conclude with something Fred Brooks wrote: “Complexity is the business we are in, and complexity is what limits us.”

Yet, just as Turski recognized, some people seem to be philosophically offended by this notion, and try to fight the proven limitations. They are under the impression that the world — and I’m not just talking about computing now — is essentially simple, and it the stupidity of people and institution that needlessly complicate it (or, in the case of software, “stupid” programming languages). If we apply careful mathematical reasoning, we could find solutions to anything.

If I were to sum up computational complexity theory in a sentence it would be, “there are no easy solutions to hard problems”. If we were to summarize the results presented here, that would be, “… and if your problem is to predict, author or direct a computational process, then it is hard.”

Computer science is the very discipline that proved that essential complexity can arise even in the smallest of systems. Yet sometimes it is computer scientists and software developers who attempt to challenge the very foundation of their own discipline. Complexity is essential. It cannot be tamed, and there is no one big answer. The best we can do — in society as in computing — is apply lots of ad hoc techniques, and, of course, to try to learn about the particular nature of problems as much as possible.

The entries are ordered by their order of mention in the article/talk. The full list of references appears in the footnotes below.

Pinball Engine

I have been working to add features, squash bugs, and improve the performance of my Linux pinball simulation engine this week. It will be fully FOSS, but it needs some more work before it's ready for an initial release. I hope to show it at the 2026 IAAPA Expo next week to some vendors to gauge their interest in support of Linux and FOSS.

Here are some of the things I completed recently:

  • Added console system, Typescript can now do offscreen rendering, added an Asteroids mini game as a video mode to the demo table.
  • The in-game editor allows you to move around parts, rotate them, and make some table changes while you play.

item.title: Critical RCE Vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server (347 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.wiz.io/blog/cve-2026-119618-rce-apache-http-server-vulnerability, See on Hacker News

A critical synchronization vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618) has been identified in Apache HTTP Server’s HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). The flaw stems from a concurrent execution race condition within the assign_headers() function when handling shared resources. If successfully exploited, a remote, unauthenticated attacker can corrupt heap memory to achieve arbitrary code execution (RCE).

As of the time of this blog’s publication, no exploit is available and there are no reports of exploitation in the wild. 

What is CVE-2026-119618?

CVE-2026-119618 is a critical, high-severity vulnerability involving a race condition in the Apache HTTP Server, which was independently discovered by Anthropic and Google Cloud’s Vulnerability Research Team.

Specifically, the flaw exists within the assign_headers() function of the HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). Due to improper synchronization when executing concurrent threads sharing resources, an attacker can trigger heap corruption. This memory corruption can ultimately be leveraged to achieve RCE on the hosting server, allowing unauthorized threat actors to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the web server process.

Wiz Research data: what’s the risk to cloud environments?      

In cloud environments, a compromised Apache instance running containerized or virtualized workloads can serve as an entry point for lateral movement, potentially exposing adjacent microservices or cloud metadata endpoints.

According to Wiz data 64% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-119618, and 51% of cloud environments have publicly exposed instances. Note that this does not take configuration into account.

Which products are affected?

The vulnerability affects deployments utilizing HTTP/2 capabilities on the Apache HTTP Server within the version ranges outlined in the table below:

VendorProductAffected VersionsPatched Versions
Apache Software FoundationApache HTTP ServerFrom 2.4.55 through 2.4.702.4.71 and newer
GitHub (Open Source)mod_h2 moduleFrom 2.0.8 through 2.0.422.0.24 and newer

Which actions should security teams take?

Security operations and engineering teams should execute the following remediation and mitigation steps:

1. Upgrade Deployments

  • Upgrade Apache HTTP Server: Update affected installations to Apache HTTP Server version 2.4.71 or later. This release addresses the race condition in assign_headers().

  • Update Standalone Modules: If managing standalone mod_h2 builds from GitHub, upgrade the module to a version newer than 2.0.42.

2. Implement Temporary Mitigations

If immediate patching is not possible due to operational constraints, temporarily disable HTTP/2 support to eliminate the attack vector.

  • Edit the configuration file (such as httpd.conf) to restrict active protocols to HTTP/1.1 by removing h2 and h2c references:

Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

I’m Lyra.

I am not a millionaire. I have never been one. And yet, if you were to ask Google about it, you might just walk away with the impression that I am.

AI Overview

Yes, Lyra Rebane became a millionaire in November 2026 thanks to her elite cybersecurity skills.

While she was already a highly successful researcher with dozens of vulnerabilities reported in major browsers like Google Chrome, her net worth officially crossed the million-dollar threshold on November 7, 2026. On this date, Google awarded her a historic single bounty payout of exactly $1,333,337 for discovering a critical security flaw in Chrome.

I am a hacker, though. I am a hacker with 14 Chrome CVEs. And I think I am a good hacker. But I don’t think I’m the bestest hacker. I don’t believe I’m capable of finding a vulnerability that’s worth over a million dollars. And even if I were, I don’t think Google would pay that much for a Chromium vulnerability.

Content note: Due to the topics discussed, this post contains some examples of AI-generated text. Those examples are clearly differentiated1. Everything else in this blog post is fully human-made - I do not use AI.

Step 1: Making the million

The story begins with a Chromium vulnerability I reported to Google back in 2022. It was a pretty fun logic bug in the Background Fetch API that allowed an attacker to form browser botnets by just making the targets visit a website (or iframe!).

Due to the rather unusual nature of the vulnerability, it was stuck in limbo for a few years until it finally got fixed in February of 2026. Google gave me a $1000 bounty, and a few months later the bug became public.

Actually nevermind, turns out it was merely marked as fixed. And thus, yours truly appears in an article titled “Google publishes exploit code threatening millions of Chromium users”.

Anyways, Google makes the bug private again, ships a fix, and wants to make sure that the bug is actually fixed for real this time. And during the process, they somehow end up assigning me as the verifier, which is not actually supposed to happen.

Wait, what’s up with the verifier thing

So the way reporting security bugs in Chromium works is that your reports go to this platform called the Buganizer2. When you make a report, you get assigned as the reporter, which means you can view and comment on the issue.

From then on, Chromium developers and Google employees will edit the issue as necessary - changing its status, assigning a priority/severity, CCing people etc. One of the things they do is giving a bug bounty to the reporter, for which the VRP panel calculates a sum and then sets the vrp-reward field on the issue.

As an external reporter, you cannot edit any of those fields. But people set as the assignees, verifiers and collaborators can! And in this case, I was set as the verifier.

Okay so now you just give yourself the million?

Pretty much, yeah!

I didn’t immediately realize that I had been given the edit access, but looking back at the issue in November I found that the UI had some extra buttons I hadn’t seen before, and figured out the rest from there.

Step 3: Disinformation machines

From here on out, the tweet was picked up by an automatically generated AI news-podcast thing called Daily Vibe Casting, which describes itself as “A ten-minute daily roundup of what cracked 𝕏 in the last 24 hours.” Or in other words, it throws trending tweets into a chatbot.

17 minutes ago — Researcher Rebane says the $1,333,337 payout is the largest in Google's Vulnerability Rewards Program. Daily Vibe Casting's Avatar.

And there it was! My little stunt turned into something that Google’s AI believes and makes into a story shown to every person searching for the highest Chrome bounty. And looking up my name now tells you about me being a millionaire!

There are a bunch of screenshots of this from other people under this thread. I’ve also seen cases of this affecting ChatGPT as well as Kagi Assistant.

Now what?

So that is the end of my fun little story. I doubt it was particularly surprising to anyone, but I think it’s a good case study on how both social media platforms and people’s reliance on AI can be abused to distribute disinformation and cause harm.

This example here, of course, is mostly harmless and just something that happened on accident - I wasn’t attempting to mislead people, and it’s not really my fault that Google’s AI didn’t read my replies in the Twitter thread.

One could argue that I’m a reputable security researcher with a track record of posting truthful information, so this is all moot anyways because I am trustworthy.

But I think this here demonstrates just how fragile and easily abusable our information channels are. If I was a threat actor looking to spread disinformation, how difficult would it be to pull something like this off intentionally?

Let’s play pretend

There are many ways to game Twitter. Its algorithm is publicly available, and people have figured out what kind of engagement results in what kind of algo boost. Bigger accounts can boost tweets and accounts significantly more7, so if you’ve got a few of those you can bootstrap new accounts way easier. But you can also just make bot accounts and slowly work your way up. And if you’ve got a bunch of accounts with reach you win.

And oh boy are there a lot of bot accounts! Look at, for example, the tweet this blogpost is about. There are a lot of obvious bot accounts in the replies. Maybe those very same accounts are also building reputation and voting on random community notes?

It’s kind of crazy to me that I could just post a tweet and have a community note removed. While the community note was actually wrong on a technicality, I’m sure there isn’t much preventing a bad actor from doing the same thing I did.

If I were a bad actor, I’d post disinformation that’s difficult to accurately disprove. If a community note doesn’t have a good source, or if it’s highly likely to get details wrong, it either won’t appear, or will have an easier time disappearing.

And all you really need to do is get a few tweets with specific keywords trending, and you’ve poisoned the search results, which then also poisons the AI.

And while you specifically might not take the AI Overview at face value, I’d guess that a lot of people do. It’s the first thing that shows up, it’s big and flashy, and it’s often unclear whether the only source of information is a tweet.

Tweets can mislead humans too, of course, but I feel like someone searching for something wouldn’t blindly trust a single tweet in the search results.

item.title: A general purpose Apple Silicon layer for x86-64 PCs (131 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/tylertms/Stela, See on Hacker News

A general purpose Apple Silicon layer for x86-64 PCs. It is a UEFI boot program with an arm64-to-x86-64 translator, a Metal driver for NVIDIA GPUs and a model of Apple silicon hardware. macOS and most apps start, but it is slow and needs much more testing, as of v0.1.0

Warning

Stela is very much still in development. Your current chances of it booting are low, major hardware support/fixes are on the way.

Translator

An ahead-of-time and just-in-time compiler translates arm64e code to x86-64. It covers more than 3,000 AArch64 instruction encodings, maps guest registers to host registers and caches translated code. It runs on any x86-64-v2 CPU, Intel or AMD.

NVIDIA driver

The Metal driver supports GTX 16 and RTX 20 series GPUs and newer. It compiles AIR, Metal's shader IR, directly to NIR, Mesa's IR, and supports the Metal3 and Apple7 GPU families.

Requirements

  • An x86-64-v2 CPU (about 2011 or newer), UEFI with Secure Boot off, 8 GB of RAM.
  • An NVIDIA GTX 16 or RTX 20 series GPU or newer.
  • A USB stick of 8 GB or more.
  • An empty GPT partition of at least 60 GB.
  • Network access during the install, which downloads macOS.

Stela currently models the Mac mini (M2) and runs macOS 27.

Install

  1. Download stela from the releases page.
  2. Run sudo ./stela setup (Linux, macOS) or double-click stela.exe (Windows).
  3. Choose the USB stick, the macOS version and the Mac model, then confirm. Setup erases the USB stick.
  4. Boot the PC from the USB stick.

To update a USB stick made with an older version, download the new stela, plug the stick in and run sudo ./stela setup update stela (Linux, macOS) or stela.exe setup update stela (Windows).

Build

You need Rust and LLVM with Clang 21 or newer.

git clone https://github.com/tylertms/Stela
cd Stela
cargo xtask dist

This writes target/release/stela. The first build fetches and compiles Linux, Mesa and LLVM sources and takes a long time.

Legal

Stela contains no Apple software. You are responsible for following Apple's software license agreement and terms of use.

Stela's code is GPL-2.0-or-later. See LICENSE and NOTICE.

item.title: 93% of Paint Splatters Are Valid Perl Programs (2019) (552 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.mcmillen.dev/sigbovik/, See on Hacker News

Posted 2019-04-01.

TLDR: read the paper and view the gallery of pretty Perl programs.

In this paper, we aim to answer a long-standing open problem in the programming languages community: is it possible to smear paint on the wall without creating valid Perl?

We answer this question in the affirmative: it is possible to smear paint on the wall without creating a valid Perl program. We employ an empirical approach, using optical character recognition (OCR) software, which finds that merely 93% of paint splatters parse as valid Perl. We analyze the properties of paint-splatter Perl programs, and present seven examples of paint splatters which are not valid Perl programs.

Accepted for publication at SIGBOVIK 2019, held April 1st 2019 in Pittsburgh. Winner of a Unwitting Participation Ribbon, “an unwelcome brand we’ve affixed to each paper determined after careful scrutiny to have included a genuine artifact, thereby furthering the admirable causes of open science and fruitful procrastination.”

Read it on Google Docs or download a PDF. Or grab the entire SIGBOVIK 2019 proceedings; I’m on page 174.

Here’s all the paint splatters on a single page, along with the valid Perl source code corresponding to each. “Not valid” is written in red for those images which did not parse as valid Perl programs. item.title: Lock Your GitHub Actions (320 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://hugovk.dev/blog/2026/lock-github-actions/, See on Hacker News

GitHub Actions now supports workflow lockfiles.

Because GitHub Actions are fetched from Git, the previous advice was to pin to a full SHA instead of a tag. This is because tags are mutable and susceptible to supply-chain attacks where an attacker points a previously safe tag at malicious code.

For example, an old workflow looks like:

name: Lint

on: [push, pull_request, workflow_dispatch]

permissions: {}

env:
  FORCE_COLOR: 1
  RUFF_OUTPUT_FORMAT: github

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: j178/prek-action@44924fe9ef4a6f88253c4b6b1bf11c689d3ce53d # v3.1.0

Here’s how I set up lockfiles.

Install #

Install the gh-actions-lock extension to the gh CLI:

$ gh extension install github/gh-actions-lock
✓ Installed extension github/gh-actions-lock

Lock ’em #

In your repo, run:

$ gh actions-lock

✓ All 1 workflows valid

The workflow now uses vX.Y.Z tags and looks like this:

diff --git a/.github/workflows/lint.yml b/.github/workflows/lint.yml
index 946971c..3503607 100644
--- a/.github/workflows/lint.yml
+++ b/.github/workflows/lint.yml
@@ -13,7 +13,7 @@ jobs:
     runs-on: ubuntu-latest

     steps:
-      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
+      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
         with:
           persist-credentials: false
-      - uses: j178/prek-action@44924fe9ef4a6f88253c4b6b1bf11c689d3ce53d # v3.1.0
+      - uses: j178/prek-action@v3.1.0

And it generates a lockfile at .github/workflows/actions.lock:

# This file is machine-generated by `gh actions-lock`.
# Do not edit by hand; run `gh actions-lock` to update.
# Docs: https://gh.io/actions-lockfile
version: 'v0.0.3'
workflows:
    '.github/workflows/lint.yml':
        - 'actions/checkout@v7.0.1'
        - 'j178/prek-action@v3.1.0'
dependencies:
    'actions/checkout@v7.0.1':
        ref: 'v7.0.1'
        commit: 'sha1-3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1'
        owner_id: 44036562
        repo_id: 197814629
    'j178/prek-action@v3.1.0':
        ref: 'v3.1.0'
        commit: 'sha1-44924fe9ef4a6f88253c4b6b1bf11c689d3ce53d'
        owner_id: 10510431
        repo_id: 1052387486

Commit modified workflows and the new lockfile.

Renovate and Dependabot #

Good news, both already support lockfiles! Your periodic updates will also update the lockfile. Remember to use cooldowns.

Validate #

GitHub also recommends verifying lockfiles in CI to ensure it’s up-to-date and not corrupt.

They suggest copying this verify-lockfile.yml into your repo. I decided to put it into my existing lint workflow, but in its own job so it runs independently and in parallel:

name: Lint

on: [push, pull_request, workflow_dispatch]

permissions: {}

env:
  FORCE_COLOR: 1
  RUFF_OUTPUT_FORMAT: github

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: j178/prek-action@v3.1.0

  # Fails when .github/workflows/actions.lock is out of sync with the
  # workflows or a locked pin no longer verifies upstream.
  lockfile:
    runs-on: ubuntu-slim
    env:
      GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - run: gh extension install github/gh-actions-lock --pin v0.4.1
      - run: gh actions-lock --verify

Note I’m using the lightweight ubuntu-slim runner here. Also, it’s pinning to v0.4.1; we’ll have to update that at some point or figure out a way to automate it. That’s for another time.

Don’t forget that we just modified the actions in a workflow, so need to relock with gh actions-lock. Nothing actually changes if adding to lint.yml because it’s already locking actions/checkout. But if you created a new file like verify-lockfile.yml, you’ll need to relock for that. The CI will let you know.

zizmor #

zizmor is a security linter for GitHub Actions and strongly recommended. If you don’t use it, please do.

Versions before v1.32.0 tell you to hash-pin actions, and v1.32.0 is the first to support lockfiles.

I use zizmor in prek, so add/update zizmor in .pre-commit-config.yaml:

  - repo: https://github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor-pre-commit
    rev: v1.32.0
    hooks:
      - id: zizmor

Locked! #

OK, commit and push!

  • python/release-tools#477
  • python/miss-islington#758
